name: Mental Maths: 2-Digit × 2-Digit Multiplication — Core Methods
description: KaTeX-enabled practice for the dependable default in two-digit multiplication: one-factor distributive splitting. It also includes area expansion, friendly tens, special factors, estimates, error checks, and mixed method selection.
estimatedTime: 170–210 minutes for a first focused pass; then 10–20 minute review bursts

cards.definition:
Split one factor into tens and ones.

$$
\begin{aligned}
47\times32 \\
&=47\times30+47\times2 \\
&=1410+94 \\
&=1504
\end{aligned}
$$

It usually creates only two partial products.

$$
\begin{aligned}
36\times24 \\
&=36\times20+36\times4 \\
&=720+144 \\
&=864
\end{aligned}
$$

It makes all four partial products explicit.

$$
\begin{aligned}
23\times14 \\
&=(20+3)(10+4) \\
&=200+80+30+12 \\
&=322
\end{aligned}
$$
It is slower but excellent for reliability.

cards.term: 2-Digit × 2-Digit: When can you round to a friendly tens multiple?
cards.definition:
When the correction is small.

$$
\begin{aligned}
48\times37 \\
&=48\times40-48\times3 \\
&=1920-144 \\
&=1776
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: 2-Digit × 2-Digit: How do you handle carries mentally?
cards.definition: Keep whole partial products. For 68 × 27, use 1360 + 476, not individual carry digits.
47 × 32 ≈ 50 × 30 = 1500. This catches major magnitude errors.

Use \(25=\frac{100}{4}\).

$$
\begin{aligned}
36\times25 \\
&=9\times100 \\
&=900
\end{aligned}
$$

Use 40 minus 3.

$$
\begin{aligned}
48\times37 \\
&=1920-144 \\
&=1776
\end{aligned}
$$

Core splitting.

$$
\begin{aligned}
43\times27 \\
&=43\times20+43\times7 \\
&=860+301 \\
&=1161
\end{aligned}
$$

cards.term: 2-Digit × 2-Digit: When should you avoid advanced shortcuts?
cards.definition: When their conditions are not met. For ordinary pairs, core splitting is more reliable.
Estimate the size and check the last digit. 68 × 27 is near 70 × 30, and must end in 6.
a(b + c) = ab + ac. This identity is the engine behind one-factor splitting.
